title: What is Agentic Marketing? How AI Agents are Changing Enterprise Marketing Operations
summary: As AI agents take on more marketing execution, enterprise leaders have a chance to rethink the limits of what their teams can accomplish.
body_markdown:
**In short:** Agentic marketing uses autonomous AI agents to execute and optimize multi-step marketing workflows. Agents make context-informed decisions within defined boundaries, helping teams scale execution with human oversight and governance.


Expanding marketing capacity used to mean expanding the resources required to execute. More campaigns demanded more production time. Entering new markets meant additional localization work. Scaling content required more coordination across teams.


Now, AI agents are changing that equation.


Unlike earlier applications of marketing AI that centered on helping marketers complete tasks faster, agents can execute connected, multi-step workflows using company knowledge and established guidelines. That creates an opportunity for marketing organizations to accomplish more with their existing resources, while giving their people greater capacity to focus on strategy and creative direction.


Yet most organizations are still figuring out how to realize that potential. According to[BCG's 2026 CMO Survey](https://www.bcg.com/publications/2026/making-the-agentic-marketing-transformation-a-reality) , 96% of CMOs say AI is driving end-to-end transformation of marketing, but 42% still use generative AI primarily to assist with individual tasks.


The next challenge for enterprise marketing leaders? Figuring out how to translate increasingly capable AI into a more effective way of working.


## What is agentic marketing?


Agentic marketing is the use of autonomous AI agents to plan, execute, and optimize marketing workflows toward defined goals, with human oversight and governance built into the process.


AI agents can carry out sequences of work, make context-informed decisions, and take action within established boundaries. This allows marketing teams to delegate more complex activities that previously required people to initiate and coordinate each step.


Four capabilities distinguish agentic marketing from earlier applications of AI:


- **Goal-directed execution:** Agents work toward defined marketing objectives, determining the steps needed to complete assigned work.
- **Context-aware decision-making:** Agents use brand guidelines, product knowledge, audience intelligence, and other company information to guide their actions.
- **Multi-step workflow orchestration:** Agents execute connected activities across marketing functions and systems, reducing manual coordination and handoffs.
- **Governed autonomy:** Agents operate within defined permissions and decision rights, with human involvement reserved for approvals, exceptions, and decisions requiring expert judgment.


The implications go well beyond what AI can accomplish on its own. Agentic marketing changes the relationship between people and technology, opening up new possibilities for how organizations structure and manage marketing execution.


### Agentic marketing vs. traditional marketing automation


Marketing automation has been a staple of enterprise marketing for years, helping teams scale activities like email sequences, lead scoring, and campaign triggers. But these systems generally operate according to predefined rules, with marketers responsible for designing the steps and coordinating work beyond those automated sequences.


Agentic marketing expands what organizations can delegate to AI. Instead of following a fixed set of instructions, AI agents can interpret objectives, determine appropriate next steps, and execute connected activities using available context. This introduces a greater degree of autonomy across the marketing lifecycle.


Capability Traditional marketing automation Agentic marketing


Execution Follows predefined rules and triggers Executes multi-step work toward defined goals


Decision-making Relies on predetermined conditions Makes context-informed decisions within authorized boundaries


Workflows Automates specific activities Connects activities across broader workflows


Human involvement Marketers initiate and coordinate much of the work Marketers set direction and oversee consequential decisions


Optimization Relies on predefined rules or manual adjustments Identifies opportunities and executes authorized improvements


Take a global product launch. A marketer using traditional AI tools might generate email copy, draft social posts, and translate campaign materials into different languages. But someone still has to prompt the AI for each deliverable, share the right product information, coordinate with regional teams, and make sure everything is ready for launch.


With agentic marketing, much of that work can happen within a single workflow. Once the strategy and messaging are approved, agents can create campaign materials, tailor them for different markets, check them against brand guidelines, and flag anything that needs a closer look.


For global marketing teams, agentic capabilities can mean faster time to market and the ability to launch campaigns in more markets without adding weeks of production work or additional layers of coordination.


## How AI agents are changing enterprise marketing


The impact of agentic marketing extends beyond individual use cases. It raises important questions about how organizations structure teams, coordinate execution, and define responsibilities.


### 1. Marketing execution becomes less dependent on headcount


AI agents are allowing marketing teams to take on more work without adding the same level of production resources or coordination. Content teams can produce and adapt assets across more campaigns, while regional marketers can focus on market-specific requirements rather than recreating materials from scratch.


For example, a demand generation team could use agents to develop audience-specific campaign variations from a single approved brief, reaching more segments without managing a separate production process for each one.


With Jasper, teams can use shared company knowledge in Jasper IQ to give purpose-built agents the context they need to produce accurate, on-brand campaign content.


Marketing specialists still provide the expertise that shapes the work, but they can apply that expertise across more campaigns without taking on the same amount of manual production.


### 2. Workflow design becomes a competitive advantage


Faster content production only goes so far when the work still moves through lengthy approval processes.


An AI agent might prepare campaign assets in minutes, only for those assets to spend days moving between teams. The time saved in production gets lost in the handoffs that follow.


Many of these processes were designed when people had to execute every step manually. As agents take on more of that work, marketing leaders have an opportunity to reconsider which steps are still necessary.


[McKinsey research](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/people-and-organization/our-insights/from-adoption-to-impact-three-horizons-of-ai-transformation) found that organizations redesigning workflows around AI were 5.3 times more likely to report capturing enterprise-level value than those leaving workflows unchanged.


For marketing teams, redesign might mean allowing agents to conduct research and develop channel variations in parallel, using the same approved context. Routine approvals can be reduced when agents operate within established guidelines, while decisions that carry greater risk remain subject to human review.


The result is less time spent coordinating work between teams and a faster path from strategy to launch.


### 3. Marketing roles shift toward direction and judgment


As agents take on more production work, marketing specialists have more time to focus on the decisions that require their expertise.


Content marketers can devote more attention to editorial strategy and creative quality. Demand generation teams can focus on campaign decisions and optimization. Marketing operations professionals may take on greater responsibility for configuring agent workflows and monitoring how well they perform.


Several skills become especially important as these responsibilities evolve:


- **Strategic judgment:** Determining which opportunities deserve attention and where resources should be invested.
- **Creative thinking and taste:** Recognizing strong ideas, maintaining differentiation, and improving the quality of agent-produced work.
- **Agent direction:** Translating marketing objectives into clear instructions and defining what successful execution looks like.
- **Quality evaluation:** Identifying when work requires human intervention and using feedback to improve future execution.


For marketing leaders, these changes should inform how roles are defined, how employees are developed, and how their contributions are evaluated.


## What does it take to scale agentic marketing?


The more responsibility AI agents take on, the more important it becomes to give them the right foundation. An agent might be capable of producing hundreds of content variations, but if it's working from outdated product information or inconsistent brand guidelines, it can multiply mistakes just as quickly.


For enterprise marketing leaders, scaling agentic AI starts with understanding where existing systems and processes may fall short.


### 1. Start with the information agents rely on


Most marketing organizations have valuable company knowledge scattered across documents, platforms, and teams. Before expanding agent execution, identify which information needs to be accessible across workflows and who is responsible for keeping it current. Approved product claims, brand standards, and audience insights should be maintained in a way that agents can reliably reference.


### 2. Define what agents can do independently


Autonomy should reflect the risk of the activity. An agent adapting approved messaging for another channel may need little oversight, while changes to product positioning or regulated claims should trigger human review. Document these decision rights within each workflow so teams know exactly when intervention is required.


### 3. Build quality controls into execution


Relying on marketers to catch mistakes after content is generated can create the same bottlenecks teams are trying to eliminate. Establish standards that agents can check during execution, along with clear escalation paths for work that requires expert judgment.


### 4. Make someone accountable for the workflow


Every agent-driven process needs a human owner responsible for monitoring results, addressing recurring issues, and improving instructions over time. As agents take on more work, this ownership becomes increasingly important to maintaining quality and reliability.


## Building the agentic marketing organization


AI agents are giving enterprise marketing teams the ability to take on more ambitious work, move faster across markets, and make better use of their people's expertise. For marketing leaders, the next step is building an organization that can put those capabilities to work at scale.


There's still a long way to go.[According to Deloitte](https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/insights/industry/technology/path-to-agentic-transformation.html) , 74% of business and IT leaders expect nearly half their business processes to be redesigned around AI agents within four years, yet only 5% say their processes are highly prepared.
